3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household code (wives and husbands, vv. 1–7), calls the whole community to the posture of suffering love (vv. 8–17), and then grounds everything in the most theologically dense paragraph of the letter (vv. 18–22): Christ's death, his proclamation to the imprisoned spirits, his resurrection, and his ascension to the right hand of God with all authorities subject to him. The movement is from the household to the cosmos: Christ's victory over every power is the ultimate ground of the believer's endurance in any form of unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter gives wives a long word (vv.1–6) and husbands a short but weighty one (v.7). The fuller treatment of wives fits the hard reality: in that world a wife had the least freedom and bore the sharpest cost of her faith — especially one married to an unbelieving husband. His counsel is neither a cage nor a revolution; it is evangelistic strategy. The wife who cannot preach to her husband may win him another way — by the quiet power of a transformed life.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Joint heirs of the grace of life' (synklēronomoi charitos zōēs, v. 7) — the most theologically decisive phrase in the passage. Whatever social asymmetry exists in the marriage relationship, before God both husband and wife are equal heirs. The social role does not determine the spiritual standing. Reformed theology has consistently insisted on both realities simultaneously: genuine role-differentiation within marriage and full equality before God. The husband who fails to treat his wife as a joint heir is treating her as something less than what God has made her — and it will hinder his prayers.
verseByVerse.examples: 'So that they may be won without a word' (v. 1) — this is not a prohibition on wives speaking about faith; it is the recognition that in a household where the husband has heard the words and remained unconvinced, more words are not the primary instrument. The conduct that reflects genuine transformation is. A wife whose faith makes her more loving, more patient, more joyful in difficulty than she would otherwise be — that is a living argument. Then: women in Roman households whose faith was socially threatening. Now: any believer in a close relationship with an unbeliever — the same principle applies: character speaks when words have been heard and not yet received.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct. Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious… Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Won without a word by the conduct of their wives' — Peter's strategy is striking: a husband who will not listen to the gospel spoken may be won by the gospel lived. So he turns the wife's energy from the outside to the inside. Let your adornment be 'not external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold' — he is not banning jewelry but refusing to let a woman's worth hang on it — 'but the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.' There is that word imperishable again (1:4, 23): the world's beauty fades; this beauty lasts, and God treasures it.

'A gentle and quiet spirit' is easily misheard. 'Gentle' (praus) is the very word Jesus uses of himself — 'I am gentle and lowly in heart' (Matt 11:29) — and it is not timidity but strength under control, power that does not need to assert itself. 'Quiet' is the settled calm that is free from the anxious need to display and defend the self.

Then a short, heavy word to husbands: 'live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel.' 'Weaker vessel' is no comment on her faith, wisdom, or standing before God — in the very next breath she is his equal, an 'heir with you of the grace of life.' It almost certainly means physically weaker, and the point cuts the opposite way from how it is often heard: greater strength is not a license but an obligation — to honor and protect, never to exploit. And the stakes are startling: a husband who dishonors his wife will find 'your prayers may [be] hindered.' How a man treats his wife reaches all the way up to his communion with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter speaks first to the whole church (vv.8–12), then to the particular pain of unjust suffering (vv.13–17). The movement is deliberate: a community marked by unity, sympathy, and tender humility, meeting pressure from outside, finds that the pressure itself opens a door — 'always be prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for the reason for the hope that is in you.' Inner health and outward witness are of one piece.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts' (kyrion de ton Christon hagiasate en tais kardiais hymōn, v. 15) — the verb hagiazō (to sanctify, to set apart as holy) is the same verb used for making the temple and its instruments holy. Peter calls believers to make Christ the holy center of their inner life — the one around whom everything else is ordered. This is the precondition for the apologia that follows: you can only give an account of the hope within you if Christ is truly the Lord of the inner life, not a peripheral addition to it.
verseByVerse.examples: 'Always being prepared to make a defense' (v. 15) — the word apologia (defense, formal answer to a charge — from which English gets 'apologetics') was a legal term for the defendant's formal reply in court. Peter is addressing every believer, not only trained theologians: everyone should be prepared to explain their hope. 'With gentleness and respect' (meta prautētos kai phobou) — the manner of the defense is as important as its content. An apologia delivered with contempt for the questioner defeats its own purpose. The hope that drives the answer must be visible in the way the answer is given.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing. For 'Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter names five family traits of a church that will suffer well together: 'unity of mind' (they read their situation the same way), 'sympathy' (they feel one another's pain), 'brotherly love' (they are bound together), 'a tender heart' (they move toward one another's need), and 'a humble mind' (no one nurses his own suffering as more important than his brother's). This is the fellowship that survives a furnace — not a crowd of individuals, but a body.

And toward those outside who wound them: 'do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless.' It overturns the whole human reflex, echoing Jesus' own command to bless those who curse you (Luke 6:28). To seal it Peter quotes Psalm 34: 'the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer.' The suffering believer is not overlooked; he is watched over and heard by the only One who finally matters — and 'the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.'

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Have no fear of them, nor be troubled' — Peter is quoting Isaiah 8, where the prophet is told not to fear what everyone else fears but to treat the LORD of hosts as holy. Watch what Peter does with it: where Isaiah says 'the LORD of hosts,' he writes 'Christ the Lord' — Jesus is that LORD. The cure for the fear of man is not bravado but a heart that sets Christ on the throne as holy.

From that settled heart comes readiness: 'always being prepared to make a defense (apologia) to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you.' Apologia was a courtroom word — the defendant's answer to a charge — but Peter turns it toward daily life: be ready to explain your hope. And notice it is hope, not merely doctrine, that draws the question; if there is no visible hope in the way you carry suffering, no one will ever ask. Two things must mark the answer: 'gentleness and respect' — the person who argues for the gospel of grace with contempt for the questioner has already contradicted it — and 'a good conscience,' a life that matches the claim, which leaves the slanderer nothing to grip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and His Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This paragraph is the theological summit of the letter — and it holds its most disputed sentence. Peter grounds the call to suffer for righteousness in the ultimate case: Christ 'suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God.' Then, in compressed and mysterious language, he speaks of a proclamation to 'the spirits in prison,' and ends at the ascension, every power subject to Christ. Whatever the difficulty of the middle, the frame is clear and steadying: the One who suffered now reigns, and suffering for righteousness is never the end of the story.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Baptism… now saves you' (v. 21) — the most direct statement on baptism in Peter's letters, and the most debated. Peter himself provides the interpretive key: 'not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience' (eperōtēma eis theon syneidēseōs agathēs). Eperōtēma is a formal legal term: a question put to a party for binding response, a pledge, a formal appeal. The saving work is not the water washing the body but the conscience's genuine appeal to God — of which baptism is the appointed sign and seal. Rome and Orthodoxy read 'saves you' as baptismal regeneration by the act itself (ex opere operato); the Reformed tradition reads baptism as the sign of the covenant promise, saving as the instrument through which the Spirit seals the conscience's faith-appeal to God. Peter's own qualifier makes the latter reading the more natural one: the dirt-washing is explicitly set aside; the appeal is what saves.
verseByVerse.examples: The spirits-in-prison passage has generated more commentary than almost any other NT text. The preacher must name the major options honestly, identify the strongest, and not pretend to a certainty the text does not provide. What the passage unambiguously teaches is Christ's cosmic victory: the one who was put to death is now at the right hand of God with angels, authorities, and powers subject to him. That is the ground of the believer's endurance. The details of v. 19 are secondary to this central claim. Then: scattered exiles wondering whether the powers that oppress them will ever be held to account. Now: the same question in every generation — and the same answer: the ascended Christ already holds every power subject to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit, in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water. Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Begin with the glory of it: 'Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.' Every word bears weight. 'Once' (hapax) — once for all; this sacrifice can never be repeated and never needs to be. 'The righteous for the unrighteous' — the innocent in the place of the guilty, the great exchange. And the goal is not merely our pardon but our homecoming: 'to bring us to God.'

Then the hard sentence: he 'went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey… in the days of Noah.' Christians have read it in three main ways: that between his death and resurrection Christ proclaimed to the imprisoned spirits of Noah's generation (the reading behind 'he descended' in the creed); that Christ preached through Noah, by his Spirit, to the people of Noah's own day, who are now long dead; or that the risen, ascending Christ announced his victory over the fallen spiritual powers imprisoned since Noah's time. That last reading fits the flow well — death (v.18), then proclamation (v.19), then ascension and the subjection of 'angels, authorities, and powers' (v.22) — taking the proclamation as a conqueror's announcement of triumph rather than an offer of the gospel. It is an honest difficulty, and certainty here is not on offer; but the thing Peter is certain of is unmistakable: Christ is risen, ascended, and enthroned, every power in the universe now under his feet.

Finally, 'baptism… now saves you.' Peter guards the phrase at once: 'not as a removal of dirt from the body' — not the water itself — 'but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.' The flood was the picture; baptism answers to it as the sign of a heart's genuine appeal to God. What saves is not the washing but the risen Christ to whom it points.

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to the theme of suffering but with a new theological frame: the end of all things is at hand (v. 7), so suffering must be understood eschatologically. The first half (vv. 1–11) grounds the break with the old life and the obligations of the new community in the nearness of the end. The second half (vv. 12–19) addresses the 'fiery trial' directly: do not be surprised by it; it is the expected furnace-testing of the gospel age; rejoice to share Christ's sufferings; and commit yourselves to the faithful Creator. The chapter is the letter's most direct pastoral address to a suffering community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Manifold Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The decisive break with the old life (vv.1–6) gives way to a warm picture of community life in the last days (vv.7–11). A people who have suffered with Christ have made the great turn; the time that remains is to be spent for the will of God. And the gifts God has handed to every member are the very instruments through which his 'manifold grace' — grace of many colors — becomes visible to a watching world.
verseByVerse.theology: 'Each has received a gift' (charisma, v. 10) — the distribution is universal, not restricted to a spiritual elite. Peter's two categories (speaking and serving) are the broadest possible taxonomy: everything a believer does for the community falls into one or the other. 'As good stewards of God's varied grace' (oikonomoi poikilēs charitos theou) — poikilēs (varied, many-colored, variegated) suggests a tapestry or the varied patterns of nature; the grace of God is not monotone but a rich multiplicity expressed differently through every gift. The steward does not own the gift; he manages it on behalf of the owner.
verseByVerse.examples: 'The end of all things is at hand' (v. 7) is the eschatological sobriety that concentrates priorities. Peter does not give a timetable; he describes a posture: clear-headed, prayerful, hospitable, actively serving with whatever gift has been given. These are exactly the behaviors that become difficult when people are distracted by the cares of the present age. The nearness of the end is not a reason for withdrawal but a reason for intensified engagement — specifically in the community where grace is distributed and expressed.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God. For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you…
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking.' The word 'arm' is military: Christ's mindset toward suffering — entrusting himself to the Father rather than striking back (2:23) — is a weapon to be strapped on before the battle. And the one who has followed Christ into suffering rather than compromise 'has ceased from sin': not that the pain earns forgiveness, but that a willingness to suffer for righteousness rather than sin proves the decisive break has been made. So live 'no longer for human passions but for the will of God.' Peter is blunt: 'the time that is past suffices' for the old round of 'sensuality, passions, drunkenness' — enough of your life has already been poured out there; not another day is owed to it.

And do not be thrown when your old companions turn hostile: 'they are surprised when you do not join them… and they malign you.' The word for 'surprised' means they think you strange, a foreigner — which is exactly what you now are, an exile whose strangeness to the world proves your belonging to God.

Then the letter's most puzzling line: 'the gospel was preached even to those who are dead' (v.6). It is best read simply: 'those who are dead' describes their state now — believers who heard the gospel while they lived and have since died. The point is pastoral, and precious to a persecuted church burying its own: the gospel that reached them did its saving work, and death cannot undo it. Though they were 'judged in the flesh the way people are' — they died, some perhaps as martyrs — they now 'live in the spirit the way God does.' Death is not the last word over anyone who has heard and believed.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers. Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling. As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies — in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The end of all things is at hand' — and Peter draws from it not panic but clear-headed love. Because the end presses in, 'be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers'; 'above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins' (Prov 10:12) — the love that absorbs an offense rather than broadcasting it. 'Show hospitality… without grumbling' — open your home, and do not poison the gift with resentment.

Then the principle for every believer's gift: 'as each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace.' 'Varied' (poikilēs) means many-colored, like an embroidered cloth — God's grace is not poured through identical people but through the whole spectrum of the church's members. Peter names two broad kinds: 'whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God' — let the one who teaches feel the weight of it, as though God himself were speaking — and 'whoever serves, [by] the strength that God supplies.' Even our serving runs on his power, not ours, 'in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.' That is the aim of every gift: not our reputation, but his glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Peter faces the 'fiery trial' head-on: do not be surprised by it, as though something strange were happening — it is the expected furnace of the gospel age. The paragraph moves from that command (v.12), to the call to rejoice as sharers in Christ's sufferings (v.13), to the promise of the Spirit resting on the insulted believer (v.14), to the difference between suffering as a criminal and suffering as a Christian (vv.15–16), to the sobering truth that judgment begins with God's own house (vv.17–19). It is the letter's most sustained piece of pastoral reasoning.
verseByVerse.theology: 'The Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you' (v. 14) — the shekinah glory-language from the OT: the glory-cloud that rested on the tabernacle (Exod 40:34–38) and filled the temple (1 Kgs 8:10–11) now rests on the suffering believer. The one who is insulted for the name of Christ is the new locus of God's glorious presence. The suffering does not mark the absence of God; it marks the most intense presence of God. This is the letter's most astonishing promise: the believer under fire is more fully inhabited by divine glory than the comfortable believer who has never been tested.
verseByVerse.examples: 'If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed' (v. 14) — the beatitude form of Jesus (Matt 5:11–12) applied to the readers' specific situation. The insult is not the end of the story; it is the occasion for the Spirit's resting. The preacher who uses this text should be precise: Peter is not promising that all suffering is the Spirit's sign, only suffering for the name of Christ (vv. 15–16 explicitly exclude suffering for wrongdoing). The distinction matters for pastoral care: not every hard experience is a badge of honor; only suffering that comes specifically because of faithfulness to Christ carries this promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed. If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Do not be surprised at the fiery trial… as though something strange were happening to you.' The word for 'fiery trial' (pyrōsis) is the smelting-furnace that tests metal by fire — and the fire does not destroy real faith, it refines and proves it (1:7). And 'strange' echoes the whole letter's 'sojourner' theme: do not be disoriented by suffering as though you were foreigners to it — you were told to expect it.

More than that: 'rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings.' The believer's suffering is a genuine fellowship (koinōnia) with Christ's own — not the same suffering, but real participation in it, and the road that shares his suffering will share his glory. And a stunning promise for the insulted: 'the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.' The verb 'rests' is the word for the glory-cloud settling on the tabernacle — the suffering believer becomes the very place where God's glory-presence takes up residence.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but let him glorify God in that name. For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?… Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter draws a sharp line: if you suffer, let it never be 'as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer' — there is no honor in that — 'yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed but glorify God in that name.' The name 'Christian' was likely first thrown as an insult — 'Christ's lackey,' the way Caesar's slaves were 'Caesar's men' — and Peter tells them to wear it as a badge of honor.

Then a solemn word: 'it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God.' The very suffering the churches endure is God's own refining judgment, beginning at his own house (Ezek 9:6) — and if it begins with the beloved, 'what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel?' The believer's fire is purifying, not punishing; but it is a warning to a watching world. So the response is settled: 'let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.' The God who made everything out of nothing can be trusted to keep whatever is handed to him — and that trust shows itself not in passive retreat but in going on doing good.

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The final chapter gathers the letter's ethical threads into three movements: the elders who are to shepherd (vv. 1–5), the whole community that is to humble itself under God's mighty hand and resist the devil (vv. 6–11), and the closing greetings that locate the letter in Rome and identify its bearers (vv. 12–14). The climax is one of the most beautiful benedictions in the NT: the God of all grace who called you to his eternal glory in Christ will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you (v. 10). The letter that began with scattered exiles ends with the promise that the God who scattered nothing — who chose them before the foundation of the world — will bring everything to completion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders not as an apostle pulling rank but as 'a fellow elder' and 'a witness of the sufferings of Christ' — one of them, standing alongside. His charge for elder ministry comes in three contrasting pairs: not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not domineering but by example. Each names a real corruption of ministry and sets the gospel alternative against it.
verseByVerse.theology: 'The chief Shepherd' (archipoimenos, v. 4) — the compound appears only here in the NT. The elders are under-shepherds of the one chief Shepherd; their authority is derivative, their accountability is total, and their reward is the 'unfading crown of glory' (amarantinon tēs doxēs stephanon) — amarantinos is made of amaranth, the mythological flower that never wilts; in contrast to the laurel crown of the Olympics that withered within days, the crown given by the chief Shepherd endures. The image contrasts every perishable honor the world can offer with the imperishable honor given by Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: 'Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples' (katakyrieu-ontes… alla typoi ginomenoi) — the word katakyrieō (to lord it over, to dominate) is precisely the word Jesus uses in Matthew 20:25 for the way Gentile rulers govern: 'the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them.' Jesus explicitly forbids the apostles to lead this way. Peter now applies the same prohibition to elders: no Gentile-style domination. The alternative is typos (pattern, example, mold): the elder's life is the template the congregation is to follow. Authority comes through character and example, not position.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory… Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Shepherd the flock of God that is among you' — and note whose flock it is: God's, not the elder's. The elder is only an under-shepherd, and the way he tends the flock comes in three pairs, each cutting at a besetting sin of leadership. 'Not under compulsion but willingly' — not as grim duty but from a glad heart. 'Not for shameful gain but eagerly' — ministry must never become a way to line one's pockets. 'Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.' That word 'domineering' is the one Jesus used for the way Gentile rulers throw their weight around — the very thing he forbade his followers (Matt 20:25); an elder who lords it over the flock has copied Caesar, not Christ. He does not drive the sheep; he goes ahead of them.

And over it all hangs a promise: 'when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.' Then, to the younger, 'be subject to the elders,' and to everyone, 'clothe yourselves… with humility.' The word for 'clothe' is to tie on a servant's apron — perhaps an echo of the towel Jesus knotted around himself to wash feet (John 13:4). Humility is a garment you tie on for service. And the reason is weighty: 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' (Prov 3:34). Pride does not merely make you awkward; it sets God himself against you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Humble Yourselves Under God's Mighty Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the shared humility of v.5 Peter moves to the single soul before God: humble yourself under his mighty hand (v.6), throw your anxiety onto him (v.7), stay alert against the devil (vv.8–9), and rest at last in the great promise (vv.10–11). He holds together what we tend to pull apart — the humble bowing before God and the firm resisting of the enemy are not rivals but partners. You cannot resist the devil until you have first bowed under God's hand; and you cannot truly bow under God's hand and then crumple before the devil.
verseByVerse.theology: The four verbs of v. 10 — restore, confirm, strengthen, establish — form the letter's final theological statement. Katartisai (to restore, to repair — the word for mending nets in Matt 4:21, setting a broken bone, repairing what is fractured), stērixai (to establish firmly, to fix immovably), sthenosai (to invigorate, to make strong), themeliosai (to lay a foundation under, to ground). The four together describe what God does to the person who has suffered: repair what was broken, establish what was shaken, strengthen what was weakened, ground what was destabilized. The suffering that seemed destructive has become the occasion for God's comprehensive restoration.
verseByVerse.examples: 'Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you' (v. 7) — the verb is decisive and complete, not gradual: you do not gradually transfer anxieties to God, you throw them. Anxiety is something you are carrying; the act of prayer is the act of putting it down and placing it in other hands. 'Because he cares for you' — it matters to him about you; this is the ongoing, present-tense concern of the Father. The casting is warranted by the caring.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Humble yourselves… under the mighty hand of God, so that at the proper time he may exalt you.' 'Mighty hand' is the Exodus phrase — the hand that broke Egypt and split the sea (Exod 6:6). The scattered exiles bowing low are bowing under that same almighty hand; the humility this moment asks is grounded in the power of the One they bow to, and the lifting-up is his to give, at his time.

And bound to that humbling is a tender command: 'casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.' To humble yourself is, in part, simply to stop carrying what you were never strong enough to carry — to hand it over, because he cares. Then, 'be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' 'Adversary' is a courtroom word — the accuser who lays charges (Rev 12:10) — and he is the predator too, awake and hungry. 'Resist him, firm in your faith' — plant your feet; your faith is the ground you hold — 'knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.' You are not the only one under fire; the whole family is in the same battle.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary: After all the talk of suffering, Peter ends with God as the actor. 'After you have suffered a little while' — little, measured against eternal glory; in the moment it is anything but — 'the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you.' Feel the weight of that 'himself': God does not delegate the mending. And he stacks four verbs to say it cannot fail — he will 'restore' (the word for setting a broken bone or mending a torn net), 'confirm' (plant you immovably), 'strengthen' (fill you with strength), and 'establish' (lay you on bedrock). Every place the trial cracked, God himself repairs. The calling was never to bare endurance but 'to his eternal glory' — the suffering is the road, not the destination. Small wonder Peter can only answer with worship: 'To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The closing names the letter's human world: Silvanus, who carried and likely helped compose it; the church at 'Babylon'; and Mark. And the last word to a scattered, suffering people is the one they most need — not safety, not relief, but the shalom of God: 'Peace to all of you who are in Christ.'
verseByVerse.theology: 'Babylon' (v. 13) is the code name for Rome used throughout Jewish apocalyptic: 4 Ezra 3:1–2, 28–31 describes the seer lamenting 'in Babylon,' meaning Rome; 2 Baruch 11:1 uses the same cipher; Revelation 17–18 makes the identification explicit. The church at Rome, writing to Asian exiles, identifies itself as another diaspora community in another empire of the age. Peter does not write from power but from shared exile. His authority is apostolic, not imperial.
verseByVerse.examples: Silvanus (Silas) as the letter's amanuensis explains what would otherwise be a puzzle: the polished, literary Greek of 1 Peter — unusual for a Galilean fisherman. Using a trained secretary was standard practice in antiquity (Paul mentions Tertius in Romans 16:22; he signed Galatians 6:11 in his own hand to authenticate it). Silvanus was Paul's companion through Acts 15–17 and co-sender of 1–2 Thessalonians; he was educated, Greek-speaking, and entirely capable of rendering Peter's Aramaic-inflected thought into polished Koine. The letter is Peter's; the Greek is Silvanus's. The historical anchor of the letter's authorship does not require Peter to have written it with his own hand.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'By Silvanus… I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.' There is the whole letter in a sentence: everything Peter has written — election and exile, suffering and glory, the living hope and the tested faith — is 'the true grace of God,' and the only fitting response is to stand firm in it and not drift.

'She who is at Babylon… sends you greetings' — 'Babylon' is the well-worn code for Rome, the great city of exile and opposition; Peter writes from the heart of the empire that will one day take his life, and even names Mark, 'my son,' the companion whose Gospel would carry Peter's own memory of Jesus. Then 'greet one another with the kiss of love' — a family's affection across scattered congregations — and the final word, the word an exile longs for above all: 'Peace to all of you who are in Christ.' The letter that opened with 'grace and peace be multiplied' closes with peace — the deep well-being of all who are in Christ, wherever in the world they have been scattered.
